title: Most adults can’t digest milk; the ability is a recent human mutation
body: Nearly all mammals are born making lactase, the enzyme that digests milk sugar, and its activity drops sharply after weaning. Humans are mostly the same: worldwide, most adults are lactase non-persistent. Where people have long kept dairy animals, DNA variants near the lactase gene keep the enzyme switched on for life; in Europe almost all cases trace to one variant, **−13,910 C/T**, which rose to significant frequencies about 7,500 years ago. Other mutations with the same effect arose in Africa and the Middle East, a textbook case of natural selection.

slides.label: of people in northern and central Europe are predicted to be lactase persistent
slides.text: In East Asian and Native American populations the figure is 5% or lower.

slides.heading: Adults with lactase persistence, by population
slides.note: Predicted from DNA; the source gives 89–96% for north-west Europe and 5% or less for East Asia

left.label: Infant mammal
left.text: Makes plenty of lactase and digests milk sugar easily.

right.label: Adult mammal
right.text: Lactase activity falls dramatically after weaning. Most adult humans follow the same pattern.

slides.heading: Same trick, different genes
items: Europe: the −13,910 C/T variant explains almost all persistence
Africa: all five main persistence variants are found there
The trait is reported to carry stronger selection pressure than any other known human gene

slides.question: When did the main European lactase variant rise to significant frequencies?
slides.explanation: The −13,910 C/T variant reached significant frequencies about 7,500 years ago, after animal domestication began. It probably originated earlier, in the Near East.
